extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate/graduate mathematics students studying measure theory, harmonic analysis, and probability
extracted.subtask_description: Lecture-notes style textbook excerpts covering Haar measure and Pontryagin duality (Fourier analysis on LCA groups) and introductory probability (random variables, modes of convergence, laws of large numbers, martingales, stopping times).

rubrics_metrics.name: Haar measure — defining properties
rubrics_metrics.description: There exists a measure µ : B(G) → [0, ∞] on a locally compact abelian (LCA) group G satisfying: µ(gS) = µ(S) for every g ∈ G and measurable S (translation-invariance); µ(K) is finite for any compact set K; µ(S) = inf {µ(U) | U ⊇ S open} for measurable S (outer regularity); if U is open then µ(U) = sup {µ(K) | K ⊆ U compact} (inner regularity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only the first two properties (translation-invariance and finiteness on compact sets) are used in the chapter; the inner/outer regularity properties are mentioned for completeness. Haar measure is unique up to scaling by a positive constant; for compact G one usually normalizes µ(G)=1.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniqueness and normalization of Haar measure
rubrics_metrics.description: Haar measure is unique up to scaling by a positive constant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If G is compact, µ(G) is finite and one commonly normalizes µ(G)=1.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pontryagin dual — definition
rubrics_metrics.description: For an LCA group G, the Pontryagin dual bG is the abelian group of continuous group homomorphisms ξ : G → T (characters).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characters are continuous homomorphisms into the circle group T; bG carries the compact-open topology (not used further here).

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of Pontryagin duals
rubrics_metrics.description: Concrete identifications: bZ/nZ ≅ Z/nZ; bZ ≅ T; bT ≅ Z; bR ≅ R; b(G×H) ≅ bG × bH.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The examples indicate how discrete, compact, and Euclidean groups dualize; characters for finite cyclic groups are determined by image of 1, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pontryagin duality theorem
rubrics_metrics.description: For any LCA group G there is an isomorphism G ≅ bbG given by x ↦ (ξ ↦ ξ(x)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the analogue of double-dual isomorphism for vector spaces; the statement is given as Theorem 39.2.4.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compactness ↔ discreteness under duality
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposition: G is compact if and only if bG is discrete.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof is deferred to Problem 39B and uses the compact-open topology.

rubrics_metrics.name: L2(G) inner product
rubrics_metrics.description: For a compact LCA group G with Haar measure µ, L2(G) is the space of square-integrable functions f : G → C with inner product ⟨f,g⟩ = ∫_G f·ḡ dµ (written as integral of f·g).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This sets up Fourier expansions and orthonormality statements in the compact case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characters form an orthonormal basis (compact case)
rubrics_metrics.description: If G is compact (so bG is discrete), then the characters e_ξ(x) = exp(2πiξ(x)) for ξ ∈ bG form an orthonormal basis of L2(G); every f ∈ L2(G) has expansion f = Σ_{ξ∈bG} ˆf(ξ)e_ξ with Fourier coefficients ˆf(ξ)=⟨f,e_ξ⟩=∫_G f(x) exp(−2πiξ(x)) dµ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The sum makes sense because bG is discrete. Special cases recover Fourier series, discrete Fourier transform, Fourier transform on finite groups, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fourier inversion in non-compact case (existence of dual measure)
rubrics_metrics.description: For an LCA group G with Haar measure µ, there exists a unique Haar measure ν on bG (dual measure) such that whenever f ∈ L1(G) and ˆf ∈ L1(bG), one has f(x) = ∫_{bG} ˆf(ξ) ξ(x) dν for almost all x (and for all x if f is continuous).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This restores an integral analog of Fourier inversion even when G is non-compact; special cases include continuous Fourier transform (G=R) and discrete-time Fourier transform (G=Z).

rubrics_metrics.name: Random variable — definition
rubrics_metrics.description: A (real) random variable X on a probability space Ω=(Ω,A,µ) is a measurable function X : Ω → R where R has the Borel σ-algebra.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measurability allows addition, integration, and other operations; indicator 1_A is a random variable with expectation µ(A).

rubrics_metrics.name: Expectation, moments, variance — definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: For an integrable random variable X, E[X]=∫_Ω X(ω) dµ. The k-th moment is E[X^k] and variance Var(X)=E[(X−E[X])^2].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Letter µ is sometimes used both for measure and expected value in informal contexts; integrability (finite expectation) is required to define E[X].

rubrics_metrics.name: Linearity of expectation
rubrics_metrics.description: Theorem 40.1.4: For random variables X and Y, E[X+Y]=E[X]+E[Y].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No independence requirement is needed; proof follows from linearity of the Lebesgue integral.

rubrics_metrics.name: Almost sure convergence — definition
rubrics_metrics.description: X_n converges almost surely to X if µ({ω ∈ Ω : lim_n X_n(ω) = X(ω)}) = 1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This notion means pointwise convergence except on a null set; very strong notion of convergence; non-example with skeleton archer illustrates it's stronger than convergence in probability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convergence in probability — definition
rubrics_metrics.description: X_n converges in probability to X if for every ε>0 and δ>0, µ({ω : |X_n(ω)−X(ω)|<ε}) ≥ 1−δ for all large n (equivalently for each ε, lim_{n→∞} µ(|X_n−X|<ε)=1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weaker than almost sure convergence; useful when pointwise convergence fails but probability of deviations vanishes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chebyshev's inequality
rubrics_metrics.description: If X has mean 0 and variance σ^2, then Pr(|X| ≥ kσ) ≤ 1/k^2, equivalently Pr(|X| ≥ a) ≤ Var[X]/a^2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to bound tail probabilities in proofs (e.g., convergence arguments).

rubrics_metrics.name: Kolmogorov's inequality
rubrics_metrics.description: Let X1,...,Xn be independent with mean 0 and Si = Σ_{j≤i} Xj. Then Pr(|Si| ≥ a for some 1≤i≤n) ≤ Var[Sn]/a^2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stronger than Chebyshev for controlling supremum over partial sums; proof uses decomposing events by first hitting index and variance relations; useful in strong law proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strong law of large numbers (SLLN) — finite-variance case
rubrics_metrics.description: Theorem 41.3.1: If X1,X2,... are i.i.d. random variables with mean 0 (and finite variance in the proof given), then the partial means M_n = (X1+...+Xn)/n converge almost surely to 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The mean-0 assumption simplifies statement; proof strategy involves forming series T_n = Σ X_k/k, showing almost sure convergence via total variance and Kolmogorov inequality, and deducing Cesàro convergence of M_n.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counterexamples stressing moment hypotheses
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples show the necessity of moment conditions: distributions with undefined mean or infinite variance can fail SLLN-type convergence (e.g., St. Petersburg-style distributions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constructs illustrate why finite mean or finite variance conditions matter and motivate truncation/general proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sub-σ-algebra and σ(X) (generated σ-algebra)
rubrics_metrics.description: A sub-σ-algebra F ⊆ A is a σ-algebra of measurable sets representing available information. For a random variable X, σ(X) := {X^{-1}(B) | B measurable} is the σ-algebra generated by X.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: F-measurability of a random variable means it depends only on information in F; examples include coin-flip filtrations and σ-algebras generated by finite-valued variables.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filtration — definition
rubrics_metrics.description: A filtration is a nested sequence of sub-σ-algebras F0 ⊆ F1 ⊆ F2 ⊆ ... representing growing information over time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commonly Fn is the σ-algebra generated by first n observations (e.g., first n coin flips).

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditional expectation — existence and characterization
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposition 42.3.3: For an absolutely integrable X and sub-σ-algebra F, there exists an F-measurable function η such that for all A∈F, E[η·1_A] = E[X·1_A]; η is unique up to almost sure equality and denoted E(X|F).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This formalizes conditioning on σ-algebras (and hence on random variables); the Radon-Nikodym theorem is the usual existence proof idea. E(X|Y) denotes E(X|σ(Y)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Supermartingale / martingale definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Given filtration F0⊆F1⊆..., a sequence (X_n) is a supermartingale if each X_n is integrable, X_n is F_n-measurable, and E(X_n | F_{n-1}) ≤ X_{n-1} (a.s.) for each n. A martingale replaces ≤ with =; a submartingale replaces ≤ with ≥.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common abuse: take F_n = σ(X_0,...,X_{n-1}). Examples: fair random walk is a martingale; casino wealth with house edge is a supermartingale; product of mean-1 independent variables is a martingale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Doob's martingale convergence theorem (bounded integrability condition)
rubrics_metrics.description: If (X_n) is a supermartingale with sup_n E[|X_n|] < ∞, then X_n converges almost surely to some X_∞.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bounded expected absolute value provides sufficient integrability to ensure almost sure convergence of supermartingales; used to justify defining X_τ when stopping times may be infinite.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stopping time — definition
rubrics_metrics.description: A stopping time τ : Ω → {0,1,2,...}∪{∞} (w.r.t. filtration F_n) satisfies that for each integer n the set {ω | τ(ω)=n} is F_n-measurable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation: decision to stop at time n depends only on information available up to time n. X_{τ∧n} denotes the stopped process evaluated at time n; X_τ denotes eventual value (defined a.s.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Stopped supermartingale property
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposition 42.5.2: If (X_n) is a supermartingale and τ is a stopping time, then the stopped process (X_{τ∧n})_{n≥0} is itself a supermartingale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses decomposition by the indicator of the event τ=n−1 and conditional expectation linearity/inequalities. This is a preliminary to optional stopping results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Doob's optional stopping theorem — prerequisites (statement incomplete here)
rubrics_metrics.description: Theorem 42.5.3 begins: For a supermartingale (X_n) and stopping time τ, the optional stopping theorem holds provided any of several hypotheses (for some constant C) are satisfied (text cuts off before listing the hypotheses).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical hypotheses (not fully listed here) include bounded stopping times, uniformly integrable martingales, bounded increments with integrable stopping time, or integrability conditions; the theorem relates E[X_τ] to E[X_0] under such conditions.
